_doc: UNKNOWNS-1 (Rowan, 2026-11-17): what the system does not know is a core feedback loop, not a side task. Improving only what is known shrinks the solution space; this loop keeps it growing by questioning the system itself. Method sources: Universal Ignorance Audit (Rowan, Sciforum 35457 and QNFO/ignorance-audit: fifteen questions in five phases, three regions known unknowns / unknown unknowns / ignorance about ignorance, categories scaffold, map-territory, protected ignorance, the last answer seeds the next pass, separated roles, 'we do not know' is a normal outcome), Rumsfeld/Johari matrix, assumption audit, inversion and pre-mortem (Klein), red teaming. `python3 -m foundation unknowns --run --apply` inventories every loop and blind-spot need, generates inverted questions per lens, scores them, files the top ones as plus items (Q-UNK-*) and records every step in the append-only ledger ops/unknowns/ledger.jsonl (the provenance record). `--answer` closes a question with evidence; a gap or new objective is appended to ops/unknowns/objective-candidates.json (probationary, read back by `--run` and by the product manager) and seeds the next pass (UIA rule 6). Lens texts follow the instrument's fifteen questions (UIA v0.3, Rowan Brad Quni-Gudzinas; QNFO/qnfo-workers research-code/ignorance-audit): `uia` is the question number; the meta lens (Q15) answer becomes a seed question asked first on the next pass.

lenses.q: Assume loop '{id}' has failed completely a month from now without anyone noticing. Write the most likely cause, then name what in the system would have detected it. If nothing would, that is the gap.
List every assumption that must be true for the done check '{done}' to mean the outcome really happened. Which has never been tested, and by what independent path could it be?
How could the closing probe '{probe}' pass while the real outcome is false (map and territory differ)? Build the case, then the probe that would catch it.
What does '{id}' never observe? Its trigger is '{trigger}'. Name one signal outside that trigger that would change what it does, and who or what already holds it.

What is the most dangerous question we could ask about '{id}': the one that threatens the loop's identity, safety or certainties? What shields it from being asked (a default, an SLA, a kill switch, a past success)?
What are the hidden assumptions and scaffolds holding '{id}' up? Name the load-bearing premises that have been so successful they have become invisible (its done check is '{done}').
What is the wobble in '{id}'? Where is the tension, anomaly or thing that does not fit (compare its trigger '{trigger}' with what actually runs it)?
What would a world look like in which '{id}' was false, that is, doing nothing useful while its probe '{probe}' stays green? Describe that world concretely.
Who or what (another agent, a different model, a user, an outside source) knows something about '{id}' that this system does not, and what would they say is its biggest blind spot?
What do we already know about '{id}' (a stale probe, a skipped check, a repeated failure) but are acting as if we do not?
Given everything recorded about '{id}' so far, what question are we not asking that we should be asking? The answer is filed as the seed of the next pass.
